blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that this is August the 1st, 1961, and we're interviewing Mr. Christoff up at your home is 34, 25. 25. Loyal. And Ralph Collins is also here. This is Bill Russell. Do you want to give your full name, Mr. Christoff, your first name, any middle name?
Well, the middle name would be Eugene. Howell Eugene Christoff. Howell Eugene Christoff.
Howell Eugene Christoff. Do you mind telling us when you were born and what part of town?
I was born 1912, 4th of July, New Orleans, Louisiana.
What part of town did you come to?
Garden District. Been up here all my life.
That up in this section all my life?
In this section all my life.
Can you tell us anything about your parents? Have they played music? Your father or any brothers or any one?

Well, my grandfather, he played guitar. All my uncles, aunts on my father's side. My father, he played guitar. Played guitar. And I had one uncle on my mother's side. He played guitar, which was Eugene. Oh. That's my middle name. Maybe after he was a guitar player.
They all played guitar?
String, all of them.
That was like a six string guitar?
Six string guitar man, and it was all his family band, you know? New family. Old family. Old family. In which he spoke good French and all of them. His son, French son. Yeah.

Did your grandfather ever play in any band, any professional groups, dance groups in particular were wondering about? I know it's hard to know just what they did. Yeah, that's true. But was it just a family get together sort of thing?

Well, they had a regular family get together, but every year they would all match. They had their own group. They'd get together. And that was string music. Then on Saturday night, it was fish fries. You know, Saturday night fish fries, they would go in them fish fries, and they would entertain in them fish fries. At that time, very few people could play piano, but probably every horn had a piano if they couldn't play a piano, but they had pianos in the horn. But they would perform a guitar. So on the other hand, when they have a fish fry, well, all night we call them fish fries and Saturday night guitars, but they all would meet up in them fish fries. And they would play that, you know?
A lot of time again?

A lot of times, all over the city they used to have fish fries. And they would have a white eye, a red light. And these guitar players, they'd make all these fish fries. And they would play, and people would be in there. And they would play up music, and they'd sing, and they'd dance by the guitar. And dancing in there too. That's right. That's right.
And that was the people just, what did they, how did they, how did they make that thing pay? I mean, did the people, were they charged so much to go in, or did they just donate for a kitty, or?

Well, it wasn't nothing to go in, but you would have to have a permit. You see, the city would give you a permit for that. And then they would come and pick up the permit. And on the autumn night, then later hours, I mean, after they picked up the permit, well, they all would get together and they would have a nice time with the music. But then if they stayed too late, then it disturbed, well, they would come back. But the idea wasn't to make money then? Well, no, it wasn't make money, but I mean, money was more plentiful. But if a fellow would come in, and they would have people come there, well, they wouldn't treat one, they would treat everybody.
Yeah. Were they charged for the dinner?
They charged for the supper.
Yeah.

But a fellow would come in, the fish fries, there was 10 or 15 women in there. Well, they would treat them all. Yeah. It's like the old time dancing. Whenever you go to dance, well, they'd play something in there, they'd play a march. On the autumn, when they'd play that march, well, everybody would march up and have to buy the ladies something. So that's what they'd do on the fish fries. And the fellow would come in to the fish fries, they'd have people just come there, they'd have a nice coach, and be at the fish fries. Well, when they'd treat, they would treat everybody in there.
Well, I think what I've heard about those is that we always forget to ask people, like Gettysburg March, they tell us they used to use that a lot to start up. Was that just an ordinary dance?
Well, that was the march.
Did they do that, say, at the Economy Hall or the Operators Hall? Every hall, everybody.

The Operators Hall? Yeah, the Corporators. Now, before the Corporators, well, it was the Hope Hall. That's what my grandfather laid out at the Hope Hall. So you could have them big halls like that, you know, and they'd play them marches. When did they play that?
The very beginning of the dance, or what?

No, well, they would play them in the set. They'd play by the Foxtrot and the Waltz, and they'd play a fast and two-step, then they would play a march. Oh, and then they would march them up. Then some fellow would come in, we'd kind of cheat. Wouldn't have no money, well, the musician would watch him. And sometimes they'd skip the march, to be sure that they'd catch the fellow that duck in the march, the man that would come up at a march. So that we'd get him that he'd have to march up there and buy the lady something. So they had apples there, you know, and so forth like that, and cake, candy, and pop, and so forth.
In the march, they would march past the table?
They'd have to march up and buy something.
And they'd buy something off the table. That's right.

And sometimes they had the older folk come there with them to the dance, as chef on them, you know. But sometimes he'd call a mother, well, he'd go by the mother or something. The father that he'd buy them something. We didn't march down. Much different from mine. Yeah.
When they marched, they just sort of walked past?

Well, they'd hold hands. When the band went, da-da-da-da-da-da-da, da-da, any kind of a march. And they marched right on up there with the escort. Then they had about three or four at the table, just serving whatever they wanted. And they had to get the lady what she wanted. But she may want the pop, she may want the apple, she may want the orange. And every time she'd get it, she may don't eat it. But she'd give it to her mother. And sometimes the mother would bring a basket. Sometimes she'd come back home with a basket full of fruit. And they'd go ahead and borrow.
I never knew they did all that. Yeah.
It was very nice, let me tell you. Very nice.
What kind of music did your family band play? I mean, aside from being string music, what kind of pieces were they? Marches or Foxtrot? What did they have in those days? Well, I'll tell you.

Falses or what? Well, they had all kind of different numbers like jigs and so forth like that. You know, it wasn't as fast as it is now, you know? Then they'd have a lot of numbers that they'd make up their self. But I used to get an old man make up song, just with words. He'd make up his own words, this song. And sang them his self. Yeah. But now, well, a lot of this stuff they're putting on this rock and roll have been from the past. Some of them words have been from some of the old time they have sung.
Some of those old songs like blues type too? That's right.
That's right. All that come from back in them ages. That's right.
The things that your father and grandfather and all, were there any of them in French songs? Well, there's some, a lot of Creole songs.
A lot of Creole songs. It's like this number, A La Ba, well, Didi was the first one to ever sang that.
Yeah.

He was the first one that started that, A La Ba. So they could probably take any number they wanted in French. And all the people that understood French or Creole, you know, well, they would sing that and they would enjoy it. Yeah.
Were there any of the numbers that, I think the music, that is, the dance music, sound anything like the jazz today, that is, to have the same kind of a beat? Well, I'll tell you. What was your say?

Well, the beat was much different from the day on the ottoman for the drums that we had and the foot pellet was different. Now we had what you call an overhead foot pattern. Yeah. That foot pellet would come over and it had a rod and a spring in the middle and it would kick out on the back. And that drummer would hit arm where he had to raise up his foot for the foot to let back. And for the get the pressure where that spring would pull it and release it.
I've heard I never did see one.
Well, the overhead, well, Dave Biddy had one and I told him not to get rid of it. Because he played with me during the war. He was the last man to have one of those.
Dave Biddy?

Yeah, Dave Biddy. Overhead foot pattern. And people would look at that thing. They'd never seen one. And then you could hit in the drum with it and hit that double time in there with your stick. Oh, I see.
You understand what I mean?
But now I said they put the ludric, well, that drummer don't hit like that because the ludric is more faster. But they used to hit that drum and then they hit in there with that stick.
With the snare stick.
Yeah, that's right. The drum stick. Get them double beats. But he had that overhead foot pedal on there. Yeah. And it sounded nice. It kept time. It sounded nice.
Can you tell us, we may go back to your father and the older musicians later, but I wondered about how did you get started and how did you, which instrument did you start on and all that?

Well, I'll tell you, I always did like the guitar. But the people wasn't like the other day. Well, the old man played the guitar and he would put it in the corner and we'd go fool with the guitar, but we didn't know how he knew we would fool with the guitar. But sometimes we'd fool it and get it out of tune, but he would know that somebody would fool him with the guitar. But it took us time to kind of catch on to the trick, you know. If we fooled with it, he had it in tune and he would know that somebody had been fooling with the guitar. But we would always pick it up, pick it up anyhow, you know. If we was going to get a beat, we'd pick it up anyhow. But we wanted to know how he could tell that we'd been fooling with the guitar. But we didn't have sense enough to know that we'd move one of them buttons and get it out of tune that he was going to know that he left it tuned up. So that was the trick until I began to learn how to tune it up. So when I began to learn how to tune it up, well he couldn't tell. So on the other hand, well after that I liked the guitar and then the enticement to get the saxophone.
How old were you when you started doing the guitar?
Well, I was a kid from the guitar, but I started outright in 1929 when I was 17 years old. So I started from C.G. Coyne and it was on Barone between Canal and Common.
Did you have a music school with it too?
C.G. Coyne had their own store, yeah, on Barone store. So I got a saxophone from there and then later on, well I come back and… What kind was it?
Better or alto?
Alto. Alto sax. How old was that when you got the saxophone? 29. 29.
And then I… Where did you go?

Did you take any lessons or did you just learn at home? Well, I started playing from around with some of the upper grade musicians. Then I went to Professor David Jones, but they don't accept what somebody else teach you. But then he took me back over everything that they had learnt me to review it. But then I went so fast with it, well he couldn't…you know, he had to accept it.
Can you tell us anything about him? I missed him in California. He's still out there, I guess, still living in California.
Well, David Jones is still out there in California. He's still out there.
What method did he use? Remember books or anything? How he taught?

Well, now, I got some old books, but maybe the back is off them. But you had to go in the method and you had to start out the method. It wasn't the same thing he wanted you to play a song or nothing like that. He wanted you to keep writing in the method.
But you still got those method books?
I got…yeah, I got the…well, the back is off. I still got it back there now.
I'd like to see them.

Yeah, okay, well I'll let you see it in this minute. Yeah, I got several of them back there. So, I like that and I got the catechism when I started. Before I started, well, they gave me a catechism. Well, I had to learn catechism. Well, I learned the music before I learned how to pick up an instrument. Then after that, well, I did start on music. Well, I know all the rudiments and know the notes and the scales and so forth. It was hard, right? No trouble. Then I wanted to do it. Something you want to do would come more faster. Then time was kind of rough. Then I didn't want to pay for the second lesson. That would make me study harder. You understand what I mean? Because I didn't want to pay two or three times for the same lesson. That would make me get the lesson because a dollar was a dollar at that time. So, that made me study harder. Did you charge a dollar a lesson then? Well, at that time I was paying 50 cents, but 50 cents was greater than a dollar.
You had more than a dollar now.

Yeah, so 50 cents meant a lot. So, I didn't want to take a lesson three or four times. I began to count upon what I'd be paying. So, that would make me study hard to get my lesson. So, I didn't want to take my lesson over. So, every time I'd go, well, I'd have my lesson. It took about twice a week.
Can you tell us anything else about him as a musician? Did he play mostly tenor? I know he made some records with Lee Collins. Yeah. He played tenor. Did he play other instruments much?

Well, according to his record, he could play several instruments. His place was a drum. Now, we have a picture of him from Lutcher, from Mr. Joseph. Yeah, he got one out at the shop. Of him, Aura, Kid Aura, and Professor David Jones, and Professor Holmes. They had a band of their own way back. And I think that was around 19, I think it was around 19, or 15, or 18. Yeah, when he was playing drums. They got a picture of it all, sir. With Kenori on it.
Yeah, Kenori on it.

Yeah, Kenori on it. Yeah, they come up together. Yeah. Yeah. So, Papa John got a picture of him. Yeah. He played in the Lutcher band. He's like the picture of his show of it. Yeah. But David Jones, he played several different instruments. Yeah, he know them all.
Was he living around here, uptown?
He lived up here for years. Oh, yeah. He lived up here for years.
You know who he was working with? Did he have his own band those days when you took lessons, or what was he doing?

Well, yeah, he had played on the TikTok there, Professor David Jones, about in the 30s. I think when Lee Collins was there. Yeah, yeah. David Jones was there. He was at that store when Lee Collins was there.
He made some records then. I just went out there before about 1929, I guess. Yeah, around in that time.
Close to when you started.
That's right.
He was at that store at that time. Lee Collins was over there too. Yeah. Yeah. Then later years, after he left, when Rainey come in at that store. Rainey stayed down during the 30s and so forth.
Did Dave Jones do anything else in the day? Have any other kind of a job, or just make a living from his music? How did he do?

Well, at that particular time, from the way that he told me that he got his foundation, well, he kind of worked it for the Gideys Foundation. He said he worked it hard, he said he worked on the regular. But at that time, he was teaching. Yeah, he was teaching. Had quite a few students? He had quite a few students. Yeah. He had quite a few students. They all knew him. He was a good musician. Yeah. Because he would be in the kitchen and you couldn't put that note on him. And he would be sitting there eating and he would take it all over your lesson. But he would get up from the table if you made one note and come tell you this is where you
made it.

You couldn't fool him, you know. No, you couldn't fool him. So we had a fellow like that down in the WPA band. And the one who played in the band at that time was Mr. Martinez. You might have heard of him, huh?
Joe Martinez.
Joe Martinez. Well, now you can be playing in that band, okay, how many men was there? And if you make a wrong note, he would come and pull you out and tell you this is where you made it.
You couldn't fool him.

He just was that sensitive. So we called him Hawkeye. Hawkeye? Yeah, we called him. Martin. Yeah, Hawkeye. But you can see in you. So yeah, he wouldn't miss. So whenever that band was playing, don't think you're going to make something wrong, then he ain't going to know. He'd come right there and pull you out and tell you this is what you made wrong.
Yeah. Can you tell us anything about the first bands you ever played in? Did you ever play with anybody with your guitar before you took up sax? Did you ever hit bands or anything else?

Well, I played in quite a number of bands around, but I played like the Tuxedo band. I played with them. Like I tell you, I played with the Yara band. I played with the Tarny Tribe band. It was by Professor Pritchett. He had a band around in the District 4th of War, about 39 or 40. What was your very first job?
Do you remember what that was?

The first job I played, to tell you the positive, the truth, was about six months after I got the horn. I played a job. Oh, yeah. And the first job I played was down in the Gypsy Tea Room. Oh, yeah. Down on Royal Street. They had a Gypsy Tea Room was down there. And the people was head that day, they lived somewhere down in the Chalmette, down there by the Shipyard. Right? I forget their name. Then after that, well, I played for the fraternity houses, the carnival time come, you know. But that was the first job I played on. But then the fellas began to tell me, because I had the music up, and they would tell me about the Green Book. See, well, they didn't want you to put up no music. They said, well, get in the Green Book. So they want you to play without the music. So, well, constantly, well, I just come, and I would have music up, and the older fellas, they would take the music down, and make me put it in my case. So that made me have to concentrate more on my music. But then when I come to find out later years, it was better for me to do it that way. Well, I hadn't learned nothing about theory until later on me. Well, in theory, well, I liked the difference between a tone and a note. Well, they tell you that a note is seen, and a tone is heard. So on the other hand, if you can see a note and don't know it when you hear it, well, it's still as bad as not seeing it and don't know it when you make it. So on the other hand, well, the older fellas, they had a good theory on putting your music on the side and using the ear. So now, if I'm not anything I play now, I go and put the music on the side and memorize it, you see, and so forth like that, and I don't have my trouble.
But do you think it's good to be able to read first?

Well, both of them is good. And if you can read and don't have a ear's voice, but we call that a wooden ear. A wooden ear. A wooden ear. A wooden ear. A wooden ear. A wooden ear. A wooden ear. A lot of fellas that can read, but they can't get nothing up in their head. A note, they never know. It's something for us hard, they don't know when they tune up. But if you train that ear, that ear is very important. It's more important, I think, to some extent than what the eye are, because I've worked around the blind, and I find out that they use that ear. It's very important. A man with his sight, he really don't know how important that the ear is all.
Yeah.

We've got quite a number of people that they depend upon the ear, especially when they're blind, the ear and the feeling, and they can tell when they get to a red light, and they be looking for the ticking in that box. And the motor and the sound of the cars stop, and they can observe that. And I work around them, and I ask them different questions, and like that I know it. Even now, when they be walking on the street, they use that stick, where they get a landmark as a guy. Then you can come up to one of them and touch him, and you can know him if you don't say nothing, well, he's in suspense. But the minute you speak, well, he'll know who you are. And I think music is the same way. If you use that ear, whenever you hear that sound, well, you'll know just where it goes and where it belongs, you'll have no trouble. Yeah, no trouble at all.
Well, I was going to ask, who else was in that band at the Gypsy Key Room? How many musicians did you have?
Well, that night I started, I started one of the old timers, I must say. His name was Morris French. Oh, yeah.
Morris French.

Great tramp-owner. Great tramp-owner player. And I had him there, start out with, because I always take the older fellow with me on everything, because I figured like that, well, he knew. Yeah. You ought to have somebody as a guide, you know. Well, I took him, and another fellow played piano by the name of Penny, and another young fellow with me. I started at the same time, the name was Dick, and the boy played the drum. We had the two older ones, well, they kept us in line. And from that on, well, they began to give us a little job, and we just kept going.
Morris French and who else was there over?

Morris French and another little fellow by the name of Penny, Penny, Penny, Penny, piano player. Little fellow didn't have no legs. Oh, yeah. But he would get on the stool and spin around. Really? He belonged to Fifth Baptist Church now. Oh, he's still alive.
Still alive.
Still alive.
He didn't have no legs.

What was the legs he had, you know? You don't know his real name. Well, we always named him, called him by Penny, Penny, Penny, yeah, Penny. I forget his real name, but he used to come to the house a lot.
Is he uptown here or something like that?
He's still up here yet. Still up here yet. And that's what, all the city was talking about him at one time. Oh, yeah?
Yeah. I wish I could hear anything. Is he still playing, you think? I bet he's getting to the house. Well, I know he's in church.
I don't know if he's playing there, but when he was playing, he was there. Yeah. Yeah, he was there.
Did he have an accident or something?

Well, yeah, that happened in Lutcher. Yeah, that happened in Lutcher. It happened in what you call the sugar cane car up there, you know, that. Lumber mill, whatever, that fire, you know, up there. He happened to hop on there and got both his legs cut off. Yeah. He still was all right, the young brother. He'd get around on them clutches and hop around good. And still get around on them now. Get around on them all. Get up there on that piano there and show up. If anybody didn't tell you had no legs, you wouldn't know. He'd be spinning around there and play a nice piano. But we had several groups and like I said, we'd always form up a lot of groups and so forth. Like the fellow knew one from another. And then we would go out jam, what you call jam section. If a fellow wouldn't have a job, well, we'd take our instrument anyhow. And we'd go out jam section. If a fellow would play, well, we'd go and set in. All that was a good recreation and then let the other fellow see what we could do. Then the problem when the fellow got void, well, they would hire you when they see what you could do. We would always go out, whatever, we'd call jam section to come. And then some folks would knock off from one job to another and then they'd go jam section.
Who were some of your favorite musicians you liked those days that you would hear? On sax, for instance, was there any particular favorite that you had on either alto or tenor?

Well, I'll tell you, there are a lot of fellows that liked me on the alto. Because one thing about the alto at that particular time, it wasn't too many fellows that could keep the melody. So they only had about three of us that could keep that melody. If the fellows knew, one was Son Johnson and Eddie Johnson and me. We'd known that fellows that could play plenty of melody. You know the leads on all numbers. We'd take years ago, well, the musicians, they always did look up to the trumpet player for the leader. And more often after the trumpet would play the lead, well, some of the sikes, well, they would improvise. They didn't know too much melody, but we had certain jobs that people wanted the melody. Then if you improvise in between, they want you to get on the melody on and off. Then you're playing more Dixieland, what they can understand. But if you just go all out with this improvising, well, they don't know what you didn't play. But sometimes you can ask people to ask you to play a diamond. Well, if this come on out improvising, well, they don't hear the melody of it. They don't know what they didn't play. But probably another musician, he would understand the harmony. But everybody would understand harmony. So on the other hand, for the benefit of the doubt, you'd have to play a little lead and a little harmony. So they can understand what you're doing. But everybody would understand harmony. But a musician would.
Who were your favorite trumpet players? Who did you like to play with? Who were the best ones in the city and all that you heard those days?

Well, I'll tell you, we had quite a few good trumpet players. I'd say Sam Morgan, Buddy P. King, and we had Punch. He was a nice trumpet player at that time. Rain A was one of the next greatest to Sam Morgan, I think, with Tornation. But Sam had a sweet Tornation at the time. And Rain A, he come with the best second tone of the city that we know. We had several good ones. And probably all of them was good back in them days. But they had different favorites and so forth like that. Well, Buddy T. P., we would say at that time, well, he was known as Bell House. And we said, it was a lot of ragtime. They called it Bell House. It was a ragtime. So, well, that's what he would come with a bucket in his hand. And he would blow in the bucket. And he'd get to the hall, they'd tell Buddy, Boy, blow in the bucket, Buddy. So they wanted to hear Buddy blow in the bucket. So at that time, we didn't hear about no mutes or nothing like that. Or no hats or the derby like the orchestra used, you know. Then later years, well, Sam had held the city for, as I know, for Sam Morgan to round by 25. Then we had what you call a contest at Pelican in 1925. Well, at that time, it was Celestan and Sam Morgan. They had a contest. Well, quite naturally, the people had never heard a wah-wah mute. So Celestan put that wah-wah mute in his trumpet. And he began to come on there with my Josephine, which it was a steal from some of these days.
Yeah, the tune and something like that.

And the people never had heard it. And he put that mute in there and making that wah-wah. Well, they give him the cup. So that from then on, Celestan held the whole city. And it wasn't soon later that Sam went on because he took a stroke, you know. Yeah. But Sam had held the city for many years. Went all on the coast and everywhere with Sam Morgan. And they would meet up out there like on a Sunday. Or they would meet up on the corner and they would get in the bucket. And they would hook them tailgates together. And one truck couldn't pull off without the oven. And sometimes the people would be cooking and they would forget that they were cooking. And sometimes the pots would burn up. People would forget about their cooking and so much music going on in the corner. People would forget their cooking and come to the window. And sometimes they would stay in the window and something could leave out of the house. Sometimes they would battle all that for about an hour. Sometimes maybe a little long. But I tell you, everybody, it seemed like it wasn't a Sunday that you didn't hear some kind of a band of music. You'd hear something every Sunday. Bands of music, dance hall was all over the city. Everywhere people was going for dances. And it looked like everybody was taken to dances. And it looked like everybody had rhythm in their feet. So if you could play music, don't care what it was, that you would welcome in any of the homes, if you know anything, any kind of instrument, guitar, a piano, well them were the most things that they was using in the homes at those particular times. People, they would like you to play guitar. Even on the guitar player would come in at night. Say sometime it would be 2 o'clock, 3 o'clock in the morning. Sometime like my father, he would come home 3 o'clock in the morning. He would get the blues, he would sit on the back step in the yard all night long with the guitar. And play that guitar and it looked like the lady got the sweeter that music sounded. And people would want to hear it.
Yeah, they wouldn't call the police.
They wouldn't call the police. It looked like the lady got the sweeter it sounded.
Yeah, I wish I could hear it.

And sometimes he'd stay there all night long playing that guitar. Late at night. And sometime my mother would see behind, oh, Louis, won't you, for God's sake, Louis, with that guitar. Won't you put it down? Say, what a similar like me running in the house. Well, I'm never lonely, but all the neighbors, they know that. They know when I'm at home. Well, I get in here all day long and I start with music. But it's an outlet. You'll never get lonesome. Nothing like that. And you've always got company. Yeah, you've always got company. All the company that you want. And then sometime I'd be in and warm myself out. Just warm with it and then I'd pick up and look at the clock. When I do realize, but it's the best way, you should take a time. When I was coming out, I would study every day two hours. Two hours I would study every day. Then I'd put it down. But like now, I don't have as much time and don't study every day. But when I do pick it up, sometimes I don't know when to put it down. So I just go as long as I'm out of the field. And I just go until sometime it's wearing me down and I just put it down. But it's good if you can take at least two hours of study every day if you're running scared or something like that. But sometimes I get in and review it, don't be in on time. Sometimes it'll be 2 o'clock, I tell the boy it'll be 12 o'clock at night. I say, well, let's knock off. Yeah, I say, let's knock off. Then we drink beer and eat sandwiches. But it's something we all like to do. You never get tired of it.
Did anybody in your family play piano too? Did you have a piano in your home?

Come and get something to drink and something to eat and they'd come in the baggage car and we'd play. Any room for dancing up there? Well, they would dance and walk out the coach, something coming in and get them up there. And walk from coach to coach. Yeah. And I mean, it was plenty of good times. Yeah. Plenty of good times. We'd play every step until we'd get where we'd going. And if we'd leave here at 12 o'clock at night or 12 o'clock, we'd play until we'd get to Natchez or Vicksburg or Jackson or wherever we was going. Then they'd sleep that night. Nobody slept. We had took them for a Chicago excursion out of here with bands. Then they had played on the boats, making them trips. The fellas played on the boats, you know.
This on the train, were you hired to play on the train? We was hired.
They were chartered the train, the organization. See, they were chartered the train. And they would give it for a profit. And they'd give an excursion and make a round trip kind of reasonable.
I remember, right?
Yeah.
So you were getting paid for the train on the train?

We were getting paid on the train. So probably you could rent the whole train at that time for $500. And get a crew, you know. And the coaches could pull. And they'd have all them coaches there, well, they would make their money. So you'd take a two and a half round trip, if you've got 13 or 14 coaches, well, you'd just begin to come. So they could afford to pay a band, the band was drawn. Then we'd get at the station before the excursion leave out, we would play at the station. And that Sunday before, they said that if the scurrying was going on a Sunday, or maybe this Sunday, we would get on the truck. And we would play from corner to corner and throw our hand bells. So let them know that they scurrying going. And everybody would get a band and they'd see they scurrying going, that'd make them get ready a week ahead of time. Then they'd have posters on them. And the people, they'd see they had a band, they'd say, well, I want to get on that. I like this band. They want to make that trip, so, so forth. And they know it's music, they know it's going to be a good time and pleasure. So they'd always get together. And they'd make a trip. Some had their homes up there, some didn't go to somebody else. Had a home up there, some didn't know nobody. They'd come up there and make friends, walk around. But it was a pleasure just to be on that trip.
Yeah. A lot of fun.
Yeah, plenty of fun.
And what were you going to say about the boats?
Well, I said we had the boats, too. The fellas used to play on the boats. They would make different trips. Yeah, but it was a different group, you know, different playing.
You didn't ever play on the boats?

Nope, I never had played on the boats. I remember Captain Cool and so forth like that. Several boys that played with him. But I wasn't too much on traveling. I would go in one day and come back. I wasn't the only one to stay away too long. I've had the opportunity to stay away, but I didn't want to stay away. Yeah, I always did like home. But if I would have left, when I should have left, what I know, everybody that wanted me, I would have made what I wanted to make. But by staying, well, I was a homely fellow. Didn't want to leave home.
I think that's a good idea. Jimmy Clayton was telling us some of the hazards of traveling a few weeks ago. Did you ever play at Milenburg or any of those places in town?
Milenburg, yeah, I played back Milenburg. Before the...
When did they tear down, I mean, when did they fill in and tear down all those camps out there? Well, to tell you...
How long did that last? That must have come way back round by round 1925, to tell you the truth. Way back in there.
When you started playing in 29 or so, did they still have some camps out there?

Well, they had a few spots where all the roads hadn't built up. You take a Lesion Field hadn't built up. They just only paved a Lesion Field all the way back, said during the... Just a little before the wall. Yep. Just a little before the wall. We had a lot of roads that wasn't built in. But I remember when Lesion Field was the only street that was going back to the lake, you'd have the train used to go back in the center of Lesion Field, Smokey Mary. I heard about that. Yeah, Smokey Mary used to go in there.
You ever play in any other brass bands, however, besides the St. John and the Gibson and the... The Puxedo, how did you say?

Well, I played with the Tonic Tribe. There was Professor Pritchett, he had a band. Did they get out and march or is that... Well, at the time when Jesse Orange run at the fairground at the Jefferson Track, where we had the band then. We'd get one night, but it was a flop. But what he had, he had something good, but if the money was to pay it off. See, in that type of music we played, there wasn't no money paying off in there. Wasn't that a great big band? Like a big symphonic band? Yes, that's right. That's what it was.
What was it called?

Tonic Tribe. Tonic Tribe. Yeah, like going home and all them big marches, Tang Heys, Part 1, Part 2. I had one number there with a 52 bar layout before I come in on it. You know that. You know that. 52 bar layout? 52 bar before I'd done anything. Yeah. Yeah, but when I'd come in, I'd be right ready. I'd be right ready.
Was that the band that rehearsed over at the Tulane Club? No, but we had-
Who was that that had the money? No, we used to be rehearsed at the Corporate's Hall.
Oh, down there. I can get stuff on that.
We used to be at the Corporate's Hall. We had Talbot, a couple of Mormons.
Is that still around the Corporate's Hall?

Still around the Corporate's Hall? Still around the Corporate's Hall. Still around the Corporate's Hall. What is that about that? There's a church now. Yeah. Hope Hall used to be- Yeah, it'd be a good-
Hope Hall. What is the address there?
That ought to be right around- Trimay or Liberty, they call it Trimay now. Yeah, down the Trimay section.
Yeah, St. Philip.
You've seen it. Oh yeah, I know it, but I do know the address.
Yeah, it's between Dumain and what? Between Dumain and St. Philip, I'd say.
Yeah, yeah. From Dumain and St. Philip, yeah. On the Riverside. The Riverside.
So that's where they rehearsed, the Big Bang. Yeah, that's where we rehearsed, right there.

Yeah, that's where we rehearsed, right there. Yeah, it's right there. Yeah, it's right there. There's only about another minute left down here, half a minute. Is there anything else? I think we've covered most of your life. Is there anything else you'd like to add? Well, I'll-
Any other bands or anything else that-
Well, I'll tell you- What you want to say?
You want the bands- Well, we had several set-ups. Well, I'll tell you- Well, I'll tell you- Well, we had several set-ups. Well, I'll tell you- For three pieces.

So for that one, we had a couple of pieces. And then we had a couple of pieces. And then we had a couple of pieces. And so forth. I had several aggregations of my own. But I would take- I don't want- The first part would start by three pieces, Ronnie, during the war. And I would take three pieces and then, in practice, we'd play a marcher with three pieces. Then the fellow would play with six pieces.
What else did you use besides the sax?
Well, we didn't use no more than sax, but we used the vocals. Both-

segments.title: Opening: names, birth date and neighborhood
segments.summary: Russell opens the 1961 interview; Christophe gives his name, birth in New Orleans in 1912 and lifelong home in the Garden District.

segments.title: Guitar-playing family on both sides
segments.summary: His grandfather, father and uncles all played guitar and string music in a French-speaking family band.

segments.title: Saturday-night fish fries with guitar music
segments.summary: The family played at fish fries around the city, licensed by permit, where supper was charged and men treated the women.

segments.title: Marches at the dance halls and treating the ladies
segments.summary: Marches at Hope Hall and Co-operators Hall: couples marched to the table where men bought fruit and sweets, and musicians sometimes skipped the march to catch non-payers.

segments.title: Repertoire of the family band and Creole songs
segments.summary: The family played jigs, self-made songs and many Creole songs, including the first singer of 'A La Ba'.

segments.title: The overhead foot pedal and Dave Biddy's drums
segments.summary: He describes the old overhead foot pedal with rod and spring, and Dave Biddy as the last man to own one.

segments.title: From the guitar to the alto saxophone in 1929
segments.summary: Fooling with his father's guitar led him to buy an alto sax at C. G. Conn's store on Baronne at age 17.

segments.title: Lessons with Professor David Jones
segments.summary: He studied with Professor David Jones, who retaught everything from method books at 50 cents a lesson twice a week.

segments.title: David Jones as a musician and the Lutcher picture
segments.summary: Jones played tenor and drums and other instruments, appeared in a band photo with Kid Ory, and worked at a music store when Lee Collins was there.

segments.title: Jones's sharp ear and Joe Martinez 'Hawkeye' in the WPA band
segments.summary: Jones heard every wrong note during lessons; Joe Martinez, called Hawkeye, did the same in the WPA band.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: First bands and the first job at the Gypsy Tea Room
segments.summary: He names bands he played in and recalls his first job, six months after getting the horn, where older players made him put the music away.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Ear versus reading music, and the blind
segments.summary: He argues both reading and a trained ear matter, comparing musicians to blind people who rely on hearing.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Morris French, the legless pianist Penny, and jam sessions
segments.summary: Older trumpeter Morris French and pianist Penny, who lost his legs at Lutcher, played that first job; the young players also went out jamming to get hired.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Favorite altos and playing the melody
segments.summary: Few altos could hold the melody; he names Son Johnson, Eddie Johnson and himself, and says audiences wanted lead and harmony mixed.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Favorite trumpeters and the Celestin versus Sam Morgan contest
segments.summary: He ranks Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and others, and tells of the 1925 contest where Celestin's wah-wah mute beat Morgan.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Sunday bands, his father's late-night guitar and daily practice
segments.summary: Bands were everywhere on Sundays, his father played guitar on the back step at night, and he practised two hours a day.

segments.chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
segments.title: Cousin Joseph, a guitarist who knows Buddy Bolden lore
segments.summary: He suggests interviewing his wife's cousin Joseph, an elderly family guitarist who knows old songs and Buddy Bolden stories.

segments.title: Changing the reel and fetching the method books
segments.summary: Russell and Collins ask to see the books and photos, and Russell changes the reel.

segments.title: Method books and the Dale card books
segments.summary: He shows his surviving method books from David Jones, Van Verricke and the card books on building chords, plus old stock orchestrations.

segments.title: Sheet music for every audience and his singing
segments.summary: His collection of popular and old songs lets him serve any crowd, with folk, foreign-language and Hank Williams numbers.

segments.title: Writing his own music and memorizing copyright numbers
segments.summary: He writes arrangements such as 'Leroy Special', copies music onto manuscript during the Depression and memorizes copyrighted songs.

segments.title: WPA-stamped music and turning to the photographs
segments.summary: WPA-stamped sheet music prompts talk of the WPA band's music, and the group sorts out the photos.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: The St. John lodge brass band and its members
segments.summary: He describes the St. John lodge brass band during the Depression and its members, including Dave, Richardson and Buster Moore.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: Brass band lineup and playing alto parts
segments.summary: The ten-piece lineup and how he played and rotated through the alto parts.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: The Tuxedo Band photograph
segments.summary: They identify the members of a 1950s Tuxedo Band photograph, including Wilbert Tillman and Knox.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: ERA band photograph: back rows
segments.summary: He identifies players in the January 1935 ERA band photograph taken in Jackson Square, back rows.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: ERA band photograph: front rows and drummers
segments.summary: He names more players, including Sam Morgan, Black Happy, Tapania and Wooden Joe.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: ERA band concerts at Jackson Square and public performances
segments.summary: The ERA band played weekend concerts, rehearsed at Patona, and split into groups for schools, parks and institutions.

segments.chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
segments.title: Night jobs and advertising on trucks
segments.summary: Public appearances brought extra dance jobs, and the bands advertised on trucks.

segments.title: Playing on excursion trains
segments.summary: Chartered excursion trains to Jackson, Vicksburg and Natchez had the band playing all night in the baggage car.

segments.title: Excursion boats and why he stayed home
segments.summary: He never played the boats, preferring day trips because he disliked being away from home.

segments.title: Milenburg camps and Smokey Mary
segments.summary: Asked about Milenburg, he recalls the camps near the lake and the Smokey Mary train.

segments.title: The Tonic Triad band and rehearsals at Co-operators Hall
segments.summary: He describes Professor Pritchett's symphonic band and its rehearsals at Co-operators Hall near Hope Hall.

segments.title: Closing: his own small groups
segments.summary: As the tape runs out he mentions leading his own three-piece sax groups with vocals during the war.
